questions.text:
The Treaty of Waitangi was signed on 6 February 1840. Place the following events in the CORRECT chronological order:

(P) Captain James Cook arrives in Aotearoa
(Q) The Treaty of Waitangi is signed
(R) New Zealand women win the right to vote
(S) New Zealand becomes a Dominion within the British Empire
options: P → Q → R → S
Q → P → R → S
P → Q → S → R
Q → P → S → R
questions.markingGuide:
The correct order is P → Q → R → S.

Here's why:
P) Captain Cook arrives — 1769
Q) Treaty of Waitangi signed — 1840
R) Women's suffrage — 1893
S) NZ becomes a Dominion — 1907
A common mistake is to mix up suffrage (1893) and Dominion status (1907), or to assume the Treaty came before Cook.
Exam tip: try to remember a few 'anchor' dates from each century to help you order events.

questions.text: The English version of the Treaty used the word 'sovereignty', while the Te Reo Māori version used 'kāwanatanga'. Why has this difference led to ongoing debate over what was actually agreed in 1840?
options: Both words mean exactly the same thing, so there is no real debate

'Sovereignty' in English meant supreme authority, but 'kāwanatanga' literally means 'governance' (a more limited authority) — so many rangatira may have understood they were giving the Crown a right to govern the settlers, NOT the right to rule over Māori themselves
The Te Reo Māori version was written in the 1900s and is therefore more accurate
'Kāwanatanga' actually meant the chiefs were giving themselves more power
questions.expectedAnswer: 'Sovereignty' in English meant supreme authority, but 'kāwanatanga' literally means 'governance' (a more limited authority) — so many rangatira may have understood they were giving the Crown a right to govern the settlers, NOT the right to rule over Māori themselves
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the option about kāwanatanga meaning 'governance'.

Here's why:
'Sovereignty' is the supreme legal authority over a country.
'Kāwanatanga' is a transliteration of 'governor' — closer to 'governance' or 'governorship'.
Historians and the Waitangi Tribunal have argued that many rangatira would not have agreed to give up complete authority — they thought they were allowing the Crown to govern its own settlers while Māori retained tino rangatiratanga (chieftainship) over their own people and lands.
This is one of the central issues in Treaty interpretation today.
Exam tip: a single word can change the meaning of a whole agreement — translation is rarely neutral.

questions.text:
Explain ONE specific reason WHY the Treaty of Waitangi is still important in New Zealand today. Your answer must:
• identify one concrete way the Treaty shapes life in NZ today
• give a specific named example (e.g. a settlement, a piece of legislation, a co-governance arrangement)
• explain how that example shows the Treaty's ongoing influence.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for clearly identifying a specific way the Treaty shapes modern NZ.

1 mark for a NAMED specific example AND a clear explanation of how it shows the Treaty's ongoing influence (not just naming the example).

Examples of strong answers:

Waitangi Tribunal and settlements — Ngāi Tahu received a settlement worth $170 million in 1998 for breaches of the Treaty in the South Island, including land taken without consent. This shows the Treaty is enforceable today and that the Crown can be held to account for historic breaches.

Co-governance — In 2017 the Whanganui River was granted legal personhood (Te Awa Tupua) and is jointly governed by Whanganui iwi and the Crown. This is a direct application of Treaty partnership in environmental management.

Language rights — Te Reo Māori was made an official language of NZ in 1987 partly because of Treaty obligations to protect taonga, including language. This led to the establishment of kohanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori, and Whakaata Māori (Māori Television).

Treaty principles in law — many NZ statutes (e.g. the Resource Management Act 1991, the Education and Training Act 2020) require decision-makers to consider Treaty principles. This shows the Treaty is woven into how the country is run.

Do NOT award the second mark if the example is not named or not explained.

questions.text: New Zealand uses the Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) electoral system. Compared with the older First Past the Post (FPP) system, MMP usually means that:
options: One single party almost always wins an outright majority and forms government on its own

The number of seats a party wins is roughly PROPORTIONAL to its share of the party vote, so smaller parties have a much better chance of being represented in Parliament — usually leading to coalition governments
Voters can only vote for one party and not for any individual candidates
There is no Parliament — laws are made by referendums
questions.expectedAnswer: The number of seats a party wins is roughly PROPORTIONAL to its share of the party vote, so smaller parties have a much better chance of being represented in Parliament — usually leading to coalition governments
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the proportionality option.

Here's why:
Under FPP (used in NZ before 1996), the party with the most electorate seats won, and small parties were often shut out of Parliament even if they had significant support.
Under MMP, voters get TWO votes — one for an electorate MP and one for a PARTY. The total number of seats a party gets is roughly proportional to its party vote, which usually means no single party wins outright. Coalition or confidence-and-supply governments are normal under MMP.
Exam tip: MMP = More representation for Minor Parties.

questions.text:
The pie chart above shows the 2023 NZ General Election party vote results. The National, ACT, and NZ First parties formed a coalition government.

(a) Calculate the COMBINED percentage of the party vote won by the three coalition parties.
(b) The two largest opposition parties were Labour and the Greens. Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between the COALITION's combined vote and the LABOUR + GREENS combined vote. Show your working.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Coalition = National 38.1% + ACT 8.6% + NZ First 6.1% = 52.8%.

Step 2: Labour + Greens = 26.9% + 11.6% = 38.5%.

Step 3: Difference = 52.8% − 38.5% = 14.3 percentage points.

Step 4: Accept 14.3 (or 14.3%). Minor rounding (14.2–14.4) acceptable if working is shown.

Exam tip: when subtracting percentages always say 'percentage points' — it is technically not the same as 'percent'.

questions.text:
Voting in general elections is just one way of taking part in a democracy. Describe TWO OTHER specific ways a New Zealand citizen can participate in democracy. For EACH way you must:
• name the action
• give a real or realistic NZ example
• explain why this kind of participation matters.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for each example IF the answer includes the action + a specific example + explanation of why it matters. 2 examples required.

Examples of strong answers:

Making a submission on a Bill — citizens can write to a Parliamentary select committee about a proposed law. Example: thousands of New Zealanders submitted on the Smokefree Environments Bill 2022. This matters because it lets ordinary people directly influence what becomes law before the final vote.

Local body voting and standing for council — voting in local body elections (or even running as a candidate) lets people influence decisions about their community, like rates, transport and water. This matters because local government affects daily life more directly than central government.

Protest and petitions — joining a hīkoi or signing a petition to Parliament. Example: the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed hīkoi to Wellington. This matters because peaceful protest is a way to put pressure on government between elections.

Contacting your local MP — writing to or meeting with the MP for your electorate about an issue. This matters because MPs are meant to represent their constituents, and citizens raising issues directly is one of the most effective forms of participation.

Jury service — when called, sitting on a jury contributes to the justice system, which is part of how a democracy works.

Do NOT award full marks for examples without explanation, or for 'voting again' (the question rules that out).

questions.text: When the price of a product RISES (and nothing else changes), what does the Law of Demand predict will happen, and WHY?
options: The quantity demanded usually FALLS, because at higher prices fewer people are willing or able to buy the same amount, and some will switch to cheaper alternatives
The quantity demanded always rises sharply, because higher prices make products more desirable
Nothing changes — demand never depends on price
Supply collapses immediately whenever the price changes
questions.expectedAnswer: The quantity demanded usually FALLS, because at higher prices fewer people are willing or able to buy the same amount, and some will switch to cheaper alternatives
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the falling demand option WITH the reasoning.

Here's why:
The Law of Demand says there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded — when price goes up, the quantity people are willing to buy generally goes down.
The REASON is that buyers have limited budgets and substitutes — if petrol becomes more expensive, some people drive less, take the bus, or use a more fuel-efficient car.
At merit level you must explain WHY, not just what.
Exam tip: real-life examples (petrol, dairy, takeaways) are good to remember.

questions.text:
Housing affordability is a major issue in NZ. Explain how the housing crisis affects YOUNG New Zealanders. Your answer MUST:
• describe at least TWO specific impacts on young people
• give one CONCRETE example or fact (it can be a typical figure such as 'median house prices in Auckland are roughly 9 times the median household income')
• link the impact to ONE wider social consequence (e.g. mental health, leaving the country, family stress).
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for explaining at least TWO clear impacts on young New Zealanders, supported by a concrete example or figure.

1 mark for linking the impacts to a wider social consequence (e.g. mental health, brain drain, delayed family formation, intergenerational inequality).

Examples of strong answers:

First-home buyers locked out — median house prices in Auckland are roughly 9 times the median household income, so saving a 20% deposit can take a young couple over a decade. Many young people give up on home ownership altogether. Wider consequence: this creates intergenerational inequality, because young people without parental help cannot get on the property ladder while their wealthier peers can.

Rising rents — when rents take 40–50% of a young renter's income, there is little left for saving, healthy food or further study. Wider consequence: chronic financial stress is linked to anxiety and depression, affecting mental health (taha hinengaro).

Moving away — many young Kiwis move to Australia, where wages are higher and housing relatively cheaper, contributing to a 'brain drain' that affects NZ's workforce.

Overcrowding and homelessness — NZ has one of the highest rates of homelessness in the OECD; some young people live in cars or sleep on couches. Wider consequence: unstable housing harms school attendance, learning, and physical health.

Do not award the second mark unless a wider social consequence is clearly drawn out.

questions.text: Globalisation has both BENEFITS and COSTS. Which of these is the BEST example of a COST of globalisation for New Zealand workers?
options: NZ can export dairy products to dozens of countries
NZ consumers can buy electronics and clothes more cheaply because they are made overseas
Some NZ manufacturing jobs have been lost as factories close and production moves to countries with cheaper labour, leaving workers needing to retrain or find new work
International tourists can fly into Auckland from many countries
questions.expectedAnswer: Some NZ manufacturing jobs have been lost as factories close and production moves to countries with cheaper labour, leaving workers needing to retrain or find new work
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the manufacturing job loss option.

Here's why:
The question asks for a COST of globalisation, not a benefit. Cheaper imports, more exports and tourism are usually benefits.
Globalisation makes it easier for businesses to move production to wherever labour is cheapest, which has hurt some NZ manufacturing communities (e.g. car assembly in the 1990s).
Exam tip: be ready to discuss BOTH sides of an issue — at merit level, simple recall is not enough.

questions.text:
New Zealand aims to be Predator Free by 2050 — removing possums, rats, and stoats to protect native wildlife.

In an extended response, DISCUSS the social, economic and environmental reasons for this goal AND consider DIFFERENT PERSPECTIVES (conservationists, farmers, local communities, iwi). Your answer MUST:
• give ONE strong reason from EACH of the three categories (environmental, economic, social/cultural)
• present at least TWO DIFFERENT PERSPECTIVES that disagree with each other
• include at least ONE specific NZ example or statistic
• reach a clear judgement at the end about whether the goal is worth pursuing.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks total — one for each criterion below.

1 mark — Environmental reason (with example/statistic):
• Introduced predators kill an estimated 25 million native birds each year in NZ.
• Species such as kiwi, kākāpō and whio are critically endangered. Only about 5% of kiwi chicks reach adulthood in unmanaged areas.
• NZ native species evolved without mammalian predators and have almost no defences against them.

1 mark — Economic reason:
• Possums damage pasture and spread bovine TB to cattle and deer, costing the agricultural sector tens of millions of dollars a year (TB-Free programme).
• Conservation tourism is a major industry — sites like Zealandia in Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi attract tourists who pay to see native birds in protected environments.
• Investment in pest control creates jobs and supports innovation in NZ-developed traps and biotech.

1 mark — Social/cultural reason AND a clear iwi/Māori perspective:
• Native species like kiwi, kererū and tuatara are TAONGA for many iwi, and protecting them is part of kaitiakitanga (guardianship).
• Community trapping groups (e.g. Predator Free Wellington) bring people together and build social connections.

1 mark — At least TWO different perspectives that DISAGREE, plus a clear judgement:

Examples of disagreement:
• Conservationists strongly support the goal and want more 1080 use; some rural communities oppose 1080 drops because of concerns about pets, water and deer.
• Farmers may support TB control but object to certain methods or worry about access to private land.
• Animal welfare groups raise concerns about humane killing methods.
• Some iwi want greater involvement in decision-making about pest control on ancestral land — and some are critical of any approach that excludes them.

The answer must reach a clear judgement (e.g. 'On balance, the environmental and cultural benefits make this goal worth pursuing, but it must be done in genuine partnership with iwi and rural communities'). 

Do NOT award full marks if the answer ignores any of the four criteria.
